Here's how a release works, and why it's ordered the way it is.

We publish a release in two steps. First, we upload every new asset (JS, CSS, images and so on) under a versioned filename, so nothing already live gets overwritten. Second, once the uploads are done, we update the manifest to point at the new names. Old assets stay where they are.

**Why upload before switching:** The manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it first, any browser that fetched the new manifest before the uploads finished would request files that don't exist yet. That means broken pages and failed scripts. Uploading first ensures that every name the new manifest mentions is already there, so the switch is a single, safe cutover.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Browsers that loaded the page before the switch still hold the previous manifest. They'll keep requesting the old filenames, for example when lazy-loading a chunk or navigating within an open tab. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would hit missing files partway through a session. Leaving the old assets in place lets them finish on the version they started with, while new visitors get the new release.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name (for example `app.3f9c2a.js`), then point the manifest at those names. Old assets are left in place.

**Why upload comes first:** the manifest switch is what makes a release live. Once it flips, browsers start requesting whatever names it lists. If any of those files aren't uploaded yet, users get 404s and a broken page. With every file already in place, the switch is a single atomic change from a complete old release to a complete new one. Versioned names make this safe, because uploading `app.3f9c2a.js` can't overwrite anything the current release is serving.

**Why old assets stay:** a browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch will keep requesting the old names. This covers lazy-loaded chunks, route-split bundles, fonts and images fetched later in the session. If you delete those files at switch time, anyone with an open tab breaks mid-session. Keeping them means each client stays on the release it started with until it reloads and picks up the new manifest.

The net effect is that no client ever sees a mix of releases or a missing file. The cost is some extra storage for old versions, which is negligible.

Our releases happen in two steps. First we upload every new asset under a versioned name, so nothing already deployed is overwritten. Then we switch the manifest to point at those new names. The old assets stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes before the switch:** the manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it first, any browser that fetched the new manifest before the uploads finished would request files that don't exist yet and get a broken page. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already exists when browsers start reading it.

**Why we keep the old assets:** switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already fetched the previous one. They'll keep requesting the old versioned names. If we deleted those files, those users would get missing scripts or styles in the middle of a session. Keeping the old assets lets them keep working with the version they started on, while new visitors get the new one.

When we release the static site, we do it in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a new versioned name, and only then do we switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. Once it points at the new names, any browser that fetches it will immediately request those files. If the manifest switched before the upload finished, those browsers would request files that don't exist yet and get errors or a half-broken page. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names is already there when the first browser asks for it, so the switch itself is the only moment the release changes, and it's all-or-nothing.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the site before the switch is still working from the previous manifest, so it will keep requesting the old names. That includes files it requests later in the session, not just at page load. If we deleted the old assets at release time, those users would hit missing files mid-session. Because each version has its own names, old and new assets can sit side by side without conflict, so users on the previous manifest keep working while new visitors get the new release.
